extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians, and scholars interested in the epistemology and methodology of mathematical proof
extracted.subtask_description: Assess whether a mathematical proof is 'pure' by determining which concepts the theorem statement invokes and which concepts the proof actually uses, and by judging the epistemic and explanatory consequences of imported methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical purity
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof of theorem T is topically pure if it uses only concepts that are needed to clarify the content of T itself — i.e., the concepts already implicitly invoked by the statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert's formulation: a pure proof uses only 'means that are suggested by the content of the theorem.' Example: the Selberg–Erdős elementary proof of the Prime Number Theorem is topically pure because the theorem has purely number-theoretic content and the proof uses only number-theoretic concepts. Purity here is demanding: imported concepts not implicit in the statement count against topical purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical purity
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is geographically pure if it stays within a recognized subfield (e.g., a number-theoretic proof of a number-theoretic theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less demanding than topical purity: a proof can be geographically pure while still importing concepts not implicit in the theorem's statement (i.e., topically impure). Use this criterion to judge whether methods remain within the same disciplinary/subject-matter boundaries rather than whether they are intrinsic to the theorem's content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity evaluation procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Stepwise method for determining how 'pure' a given proof is with respect to a theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (1) Identify the concepts in the theorem statement — what is the topic? (2) List the concepts the proof uses — which are not in the statement? (3) For each imported concept, ask: is it required, or could a pure proof exist? (4) If imported concepts seem necessary, interpret what that says about the theorem (it may be 'about' a larger domain). If a pure proof exists, prefer it for foundational reasons even if longer. Use these steps as diagnostic questions rather than strict scoring rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of imported concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: For each concept or machinery imported by a proof that is not present in the theorem statement, evaluate whether that import is genuinely necessary to obtain the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether a pure (topically pure) proof could in principle or in practice be produced without the imported machinery. If yes, impurity is less defensible. If no pure proof is known and imports seem essential, that is evidence the theorem may fundamentally depend on broader concepts. This criterion supports nuanced judgements rather than binary labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic stability / foundational preference for purity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure proofs are epistemically preferable because they reveal what the conclusion really depends on and are robust across foundational choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proofs on whether they 'reveal what the conclusion really depends on,' avoid being artifacts of imported machinery, and support cross-foundational robustness (e.g., the theorem survives rejection of an imported framework). The framework recommends preferring pure proofs for foundational reasons, even when impure proofs are shorter or easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable justifications for impurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstances in which using impure methods is epistemically or methodologically justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impurity is justified when (a) no pure proof is known (often the case), (b) the impure proof reveals deeper connections (e.g., analytic proof of PNT showing links to zeros of the zeta function), or (c) striving for topical purity would produce an argument that obscures understanding rather than illuminates. Use these justifications to temper a preference for purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between purity and explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish purity from explanatory power: purity is neither identical to nor guaranteed to produce explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof using only the theorem's intrinsic concepts is more likely to explain why the theorem is true, because the explanation uses only what the theorem is about; however, a pure proof can fail to explain (e.g., long elementary calculations), and an impure proof can explain by revealing deeper reasons. Use this distinction to avoid conflating purity with explanatory virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns indicating problematic impurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical methodological behaviors that a purity lens flags as problematic when present without justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for: methodological hyper-extension — dragging in heavy machinery to prove a simple statement; concealed dependence on choice — e.g., using AC where ZF would suffice; cross-domain showing-off — proving a combinatorial fact via algebraic geometry when an elementary argument exists. These signal impurity that may be epistemically problematic unless justified by the 'acceptable justifications' criterion.
